questions.stem: Absolute advantage in producing a good means that a country:
options: can produce more of the good than another country from the same resources
can produce the good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
exports more of the good than any other country in the world market
is the only country with the natural resources to produce the good
questions.explanation: Absolute advantage compares output per unit of resources. A lower opportunity cost defines comparative advantage, which is what determines the pattern of mutually beneficial trade.

questions.stem: The principle of comparative advantage states that countries gain from trade when they specialise in goods that they produce:
options: for the highest world price
at the lowest opportunity cost
in the largest total quantities
with the most labour per unit
questions.explanation: Each country gives up the least of other goods when it specialises where its opportunity cost is lowest. A country can have a comparative advantage in a good even when it is absolutely less productive at everything.

questions.stem: With the same resources, Country A can produce 12 tonnes of wheat or 6 bolts of cloth, and Country B can produce 4 tonnes of wheat or 4 bolts of cloth. Which statement is correct?
options: A has an absolute advantage in both goods and a comparative advantage in both goods
B has an absolute advantage in cloth and a comparative advantage in wheat
Neither country can gain from trade because A is more productive in both goods
A has an absolute advantage in both goods but a comparative advantage only in wheat
questions.explanation: A's opportunity cost of 1 cloth is 2 wheat, while B's is 1 wheat, so B has the comparative advantage in cloth and A in wheat. A country cannot have a comparative advantage in both goods, so both can gain by specialising.

questions.stem: Using the same figures (A: 12 wheat or 6 cloth; B: 4 wheat or 4 cloth), which terms of trade would benefit both countries?
options: 1 bolt of cloth for 2.5 tonnes of wheat
1 bolt of cloth for 0.5 tonnes of wheat
1 bolt of cloth for 3 tonnes of wheat
1 bolt of cloth for 1.5 tonnes of wheat
questions.explanation: A will import cloth only if it pays less than its own cost of 2 wheat per cloth, and B will export cloth only if it receives more than its cost of 1 wheat. Any rate between 1 and 2 wheat per cloth, such as 1.5, benefits both.

questions.stem: Two straight-line PPFs: Country X can produce at most 100 machines or 400 tonnes of rice; Country Y at most 50 machines or 100 tonnes of rice. The opportunity cost of one machine is:
options: 4 tonnes of rice in X and 2 tonnes of rice in Y
2 tonnes of rice in X and 4 tonnes of rice in Y
0.25 tonnes of rice in X and 0.5 tonnes in Y
4 tonnes of rice in both X and Y
questions.explanation: One machine costs 400/100 = 4 tonnes of rice in X and 100/50 = 2 tonnes in Y. Y therefore has the comparative advantage in machines, even though X can make more of both goods.

questions.stem: From the same PPFs (X: 100 machines or 400 rice; Y: 50 machines or 100 rice), the pattern of specialisation that maximises world output is:
options: both countries split their resources evenly between the goods
X specialises in rice and Y specialises in machines
X specialises in machines and Y specialises in rice
X specialises in both goods and Y produces neither
questions.explanation: X's opportunity cost of rice is 0.25 machines per tonne, lower than Y's 0.5, so X should make rice and Y machines. Absolute advantage in both goods does not mean X should produce everything.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of free trade?
options: Guaranteed jobs in every domestic industry
Less competition for domestic businesses
Lower prices and more choice for consumers
Higher tariff revenue for the government
questions.explanation: Removing barriers lets consumers buy from the lowest-cost producers, lowering prices and widening choice. Free trade removes tariff revenue and increases competition, and some import-competing jobs are lost.

questions.stem: An Australian wine producer expands to sell into large Asian markets, and its average cost per bottle falls as output rises. This benefit of free trade is:
options: infant industry protection
economies of scale
greater access to resources
increased competition
questions.explanation: Producing for a larger market lets firms spread fixed costs and use larger-scale methods, lowering average costs. Access to resources refers to obtaining inputs a country lacks.

questions.stem: How does free trade raise living standards over time?
options: Prices of all goods rise, increasing the profits and wages of domestic firms
Resources move to industries where a country is most efficient, raising total output
Every industry in every country expands, so no worker ever needs to change jobs
Imports are reduced, so more spending stays in the domestic circular flow
questions.explanation: Specialisation according to comparative advantage raises world output and real incomes. Some industries contract and their workers must move, which is one of the adjustment costs of free trade.

questions.stem: A global supply chain is best described as:
options: a trade agreement that removes tariffs between two neighbouring countries
a government rule requiring a share of inputs to be made locally
the sale of a country's exports below their cost of production
the stages of producing a good spread across several countries
questions.explanation: In a global supply chain, design, components, assembly and distribution may each occur in different countries according to cost and expertise. A rule requiring local inputs is a local content requirement, a form of protection.

questions.stem: Which is a cost of relying on global supply chains?
options: A disruption in one country can halt production elsewhere
Firms cannot specialise in the stages they do most efficiently
Production costs rise because inputs come from lower-cost suppliers
Consumers face less choice because fewer goods are traded
questions.explanation: Long supply chains are exposed to disruptions such as pandemics, conflicts or shipping delays, as shortages during COVID-19 showed. Specialisation and lower input costs are benefits of supply chains, not costs.

questions.stem: Protecting a new local industry until it grows large enough to compete with established overseas producers uses the:
options: infant industry argument
anti-dumping argument
self-sufficiency argument
employment argument
questions.explanation: The infant industry argument holds that temporary protection lets a young industry reach economies of scale. Critics note that protection is often hard to remove once granted.

questions.stem: Dumping occurs when an overseas producer:
options: exports a good at a price below its cost or its home-market price
exports a good at a price above the world price to earn higher profits
uses a government subsidy to produce goods only for its home market
sets up a factory in another country to avoid that country's tariffs
questions.explanation: Dumped goods are sold abroad below normal value, which can harm efficient domestic producers. Australia's Anti-Dumping Commission investigates such complaints and can recommend extra duties.

questions.stem: A government protects its domestic shipbuilding and fuel refining industries so that it can supply its own needs during an international conflict. This uses the argument of:
options: preventing the dumping of imports
raising revenue for the government
self-sufficiency in strategic industries
shielding infant industries from rivals
questions.explanation: The strategic or defence argument aims to keep essential industries operating at home in case imports are cut off. The infant industry argument concerns young industries that need time to become competitive.

questions.stem: A union argues that tariffs on imported clothing should stay to save local textile jobs. An economist's strongest response would be that the tariffs:
options: increase employment in every industry, so the argument understates their benefit
lower clothing prices, so consumers gain as well as textile workers
save jobs in one industry but cost jobs elsewhere through higher prices and less trade
cannot save any jobs, because domestic output never rises under protection
questions.explanation: Protection can preserve jobs in the protected industry, but higher prices reduce spending elsewhere, input costs rise for users and retaliation can hurt exporters. Tariffs raise, not lower, prices to consumers.

questions.stem: In trade policy, a tariff is best described as:
options: a tax on imported goods
a limit on the quantity of imports
a payment to domestic producers
a tax on exported goods
questions.explanation: A tariff raises the price of imports in the domestic market, making local goods relatively more competitive. A limit on quantity is a quota, and a payment to producers is a subsidy.

questions.stem: A rule that a set share of the programs shown on commercial television must be made in Australia is an example of:
options: a local content requirement
an import quota on programs
a production subsidy
a tariff on imported shows
questions.explanation: Local content requirements oblige firms to use or supply a minimum share of domestically produced inputs or products. They protect local producers without a tax or a direct payment.

questions.stem: The world price of a good is $20. At that price, domestic supply is 100 units and domestic demand is 400 units. A $5 tariff is imposed, and domestic supply rises to 150 units and demand falls to 350 units. Imports change from:
options: 400 units to 350 units
300 units to 250 units
300 units to 200 units
300 units to 150 units
questions.explanation: Imports are demand minus domestic supply: 400 - 100 = 300 before the tariff and 350 - 150 = 200 after it. The tariff both raises domestic output and cuts consumption.

questions.stem: Using the same market (world price $20, $5 tariff, 200 units imported after the tariff), the government's tariff revenue is:
questions.explanation: Tariff revenue is the tariff per unit times the quantity imported after the tariff: $5 x 200 = $1,000. Multiplying by the original 300 units of imports ignores the fall in imports.

questions.stem: In the same market, domestic producer revenue changes from:
questions.explanation: Before the tariff, domestic firms sell 100 units at $20 = $2,000. After it they sell 150 units at $25 = $3,750, gaining from both the higher price and the larger quantity.

questions.stem: In the same market, after the $5 tariff foreign producers sell 200 units. Their revenue changes from:
questions.explanation: Foreign producers receive only the world price of $20, because the $5 tariff goes to the government. Revenue falls from 300 x $20 = $6,000 to 200 x $20 = $4,000.

questions.stem: A tariff on an import-competing good is most likely to change total consumer spending on the good because:
options: consumers receive the tariff revenue as a transfer payment
the world price falls by the full amount of the tariff
domestic producers must lower their prices to compete with imports
consumers pay a higher price for each unit they still buy
questions.explanation: The domestic price rises by the tariff, so consumers pay more per unit even though they buy fewer units. The tariff revenue goes to government, and in a small economy the world price is unaffected.

questions.stem: In a market with a world price of $20, an import quota limits imports to 200 units and the domestic price rises to $25. Compared with an equal tariff that also raises the price to $25, under the quota:
options: consumers pay $20 per unit because the quota does not change the domestic price
foreign producers receive $25 per unit and the government collects no revenue
foreign producers receive $20 per unit and the government collects $1,000
domestic producers receive $20 per unit and sell fewer units than under the tariff
questions.explanation: A quota restricts supply, so the domestic price rises, but the gap between the world and domestic price goes to whoever sells the imports, usually foreign producers, not the government. Domestic producers and consumers face the same outcome as under an equivalent tariff.

questions.stem: An import quota protects domestic producers by:
options: taxing each imported unit, which raises revenue for the government
paying domestic firms for each unit, which lowers their costs
lowering the world price, which makes imports less attractive
restricting the quantity of imports, which raises the domestic price
questions.explanation: By limiting the quantity of imports, a quota creates scarcity in the domestic market and pushes the price up, letting domestic firms sell more. A tax on each unit is a tariff.

questions.stem: A $5 production subsidy is paid to domestic producers of a good with a world price of $20. Domestic output rises from 100 to 150 units and demand stays at 400 units. The cost to government and the change in imports are:
options: $500, with imports falling from 300 to 250 units
$750, with imports falling from 300 to 200 units
$1,000, with imports falling from 300 to 200 units
$750, with imports falling from 300 to 250 units
questions.explanation: The subsidy is paid on all domestic output: $5 x 150 = $750. The price stays at $20, so demand is unchanged at 400 and imports fall to 400 - 150 = 250.

questions.stem: Compared with a tariff, a production subsidy to import-competing firms:
options: leaves the price paid by consumers at the world price
raises the price paid by consumers above the world price
earns revenue for the government on each imported unit
reduces total consumer spending by cutting consumption
questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers producers' costs without raising the price to consumers, so consumption and total consumer spending are unchanged. It costs the government money rather than raising revenue.

questions.stem: A large exporting country pays its farmers an export subsidy on wheat, in a world market where the world price equals the equilibrium price. The most likely effect is that:
options: world supply rises, the world price is unchanged and all exporters gain
world supply rises, the world price falls and unsubsidised exporters lose revenue
world supply falls, the world price rises and unsubsidised exporters gain revenue
world demand rises, the world price rises and importing countries pay more
questions.explanation: The subsidy shifts the world supply curve right, lowering the world price and raising quantity traded. Unsubsidised exporters, such as Australian wheat growers, receive lower prices, while importing countries gain.

questions.stem: Which statement about the effects of trade protection on the global economy is correct?
options: It raises world output because protected industries gain economies of scale
It affects only the protecting country and has no effect on its trading partners
It shifts production away from the most efficient producers, lowering world output
It moves production to the most efficient producers, raising world output
questions.explanation: Protection directs resources to higher-cost domestic producers and away from efficient exporters, so world output and living standards are lower. It also invites retaliation that can spread across trading partners.

questions.stem: A multilateral trade agreement is one that:
options: is made by one country lowering its own tariffs without negotiation
applies only to trade between states within a single federation
involves many countries, such as agreements made through the WTO
involves only two countries agreeing to lower barriers between them
questions.explanation: Multilateral agreements cover many countries at once, so they cut barriers most widely. An agreement between two countries is bilateral, and cutting tariffs without negotiation is unilateral.

questions.stem: Which is an argument against bilateral trade agreements and regional trading blocs?
options: They lower trade barriers between member countries, increasing their trade
They are faster to negotiate than agreements among all WTO members
They let members gain access to each other's markets for their exports
They can divert trade from more efficient non-member countries to members
questions.explanation: Trade diversion occurs when preferential tariffs make a member's goods cheaper than a more efficient outsider's. The other options are reasons given for such agreements, not against them.

questions.stem: The World Trade Organization was established in 1995 to replace:
options: the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC)
the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
the International Monetary Fund (IMF)
the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
questions.explanation: The WTO began on 1 January 1995, taking over and extending the GATT, which had governed tariff negotiations since 1947. The IMF is concerned with international financial stability.

questions.stem: Under the WTO's most favoured nation principle, a member that cuts its tariff for one member must generally:
options: extend the same treatment to all other members
receive an equal tariff cut from that member in return
remove all of its remaining tariffs within ten years
apply the cut only to goods produced by developing countries
questions.explanation: Most favoured nation treatment means not discriminating between trading partners. Free trade agreements are a permitted exception, which is why bilateral deals can give partners better access than other members receive.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that the WTO has become less effective in recent years?
options: Bilateral agreements must follow WTO rules on covering substantially all trade
The Doha Round has not been concluded and the Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals
Most countries have joined the WTO and average tariffs have fallen since it was formed
Members continue to bring disputes to the WTO for consultation and panel rulings
questions.explanation: Multilateral negotiations launched in 2001 stalled, and since 2019 the Appellate Body has lacked members to hear appeals, weakening dispute resolution. Wide membership and lower tariffs are evidence of past success.

questions.stem: Which development is a reason for the rise in protectionism in global trade since the global financial crisis?
options: Trade tensions between major economies, such as US tariffs on Chinese goods
The completion of the Doha Round, which raised tariffs on agricultural products
The collapse of global supply chains, which ended trade in manufactured goods
The replacement of the WTO by regional trading blocs in every continent
questions.explanation: Concern about job losses, national security and supply chain resilience has led major economies to raise tariffs, notably between the US and China from 2018. The Doha Round was never completed.

questions.stem: Australia's long-run trade policy since the 1970s has mainly involved:
options: raising tariffs to rebuild the manufacturing sector behind high barriers
withdrawing from the WTO to rely only on bilateral trade agreements
using import quotas as its main tool to protect agricultural producers
reducing tariffs and pursuing bilateral, regional and multilateral agreements
questions.explanation: From the 1970s Australia cut tariffs substantially, including on cars and textiles, and it now pursues agreements such as RCEP and the CPTPP while supporting the WTO. It has not raised barriers broadly.

questions.stem: Australia leads the Cairns Group within the WTO. This group mainly seeks to:
options: provide development loans to agricultural sectors in poorer countries
reduce agricultural protection and export subsidies in other countries
protect agricultural industries in member countries from cheap imports
coordinate the exchange rates of agricultural exporting countries
questions.explanation: The Cairns Group is a coalition of agricultural exporters pushing for freer farm trade, since subsidies elsewhere depress world prices for efficient exporters such as Australia. Development lending is the role of the World Bank.

questions.stem: An economist argues that Australian Government policy does not fully promote free trade. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: Australia argues in the WTO for lower agricultural protection worldwide
Some industries still receive targeted assistance, and anti-dumping duties are imposed
Australia has signed free trade agreements with most of its major trading partners
Australia's average tariff rates are among the lowest of advanced economies
questions.explanation: Industry assistance, such as subsidies to favoured sectors, and anti-dumping duties are forms of protection that limit how far policy promotes free trade. The other options support the opposite view.
